priority_classification: security -- a genuine, trivially-reachable denial-of-service: any target repository under census (or donor checkout) containing a few hundred levels of ordinary nested subdirectories -- no symlinks, no exotic filesystem features, nothing an attacker needs special privileges to construct, and well within real git's own ability to commit and check out -- crashes the entire Atlas process outright (not a graceful per-artifact failure) the moment `parse`/`check`/`graph`/`systemize` tries to inventory it, in the exact build mode this whole session has been validating every generation's own work in.
gap_discovered_by: Generation 32's background security audit named this as one of two remaining findings, explicitly flagged as 'a credible, verified-by-code-inspection gap rather than a confirmed crash' since the auditing subagent did not build an out-of-process reproduction. This generation closed that gap directly: built a REAL, on-disk nested directory tree (relative single-component mkdir/chdir to avoid PATH_MAX truncating the fixture itself), then called the real, unfixed `inventory_source` against it from an isolated `cargo test -- --ignored` subprocess (so a crash would only kill that isolated process, never this session's own state) -- first at ~3,000 levels in `--release` mode (no crash, confirming the OS's own `PATH_MAX` ceiling on this walker's path-accumulating access pattern -- fs::read_dir on the fully joined path, not a chdir-based traversal -- keeps the reachable depth well under what a release build's stack can absorb), then in the DEFAULT debug profile at the same depth: reliable `SIGABRT`, 'thread ... has overflowed its stack'. Later re-confirmed the crash reproduces at only ~600 levels in debug mode too, once the intended fix's own regression test was written with that shallower, cheaper-to-build depth.
key_finding: `adapter::source::visit_inventory` (adapter/src/source/mod.rs) recurses via `classify_entry` -> `visit_inventory` once per non-ignored subdirectory, with no depth parameter, no counter, and no dedicated large stack (unlike `adapter::semantic::rust::RustSemanticExtractor::extract`, which explicitly spawns its AST-walking work on a 256MB dedicated thread specifically because its OWN recursive walk is 'the SAME adversarial-depth tree' as `syn::parse_file`'s own recursion -- the filesystem walker received no equivalent treatment). Debug-profile `cargo test`/`cargo run` -- the default, unqualified invocation, and the one every validation command in this session's own standing loop has used throughout -- overflows the default thread stack at roughly 600 levels of ordinary nested directories, aborting the entire process with SIGABRT: not a per-artifact failure any existing recovery path (`record_unreadable_artifact`, `classify_non_file`) could catch, since the OS terminates the process before any Rust-level error handling ever runs.
verification_before_acting: Read `visit_inventory`/`classify_entry` directly in the real, unfixed source, confirming the mutual recursion has no depth tracking of any kind.

Built a REAL nested directory tree on disk (~3,000 levels, via relative single-component `mkdir`+`chdir` to avoid the fixture-construction itself hitting `PATH_MAX`) and confirmed empirically (not assumed) that this walker's own path-accumulating access pattern (`fs::read_dir` on a fully joined absolute-ish path, built via repeated `.join()`) caps the REACHABLE depth well under 3,000: a direct `os.listdir()` on the deepest constructed path failed with `ENAMETOOLONG` at ~3,000/6,093 bytes, establishing the natural ceiling this walker's own attack surface is bounded by.

Ran the real, unfixed `inventory_source` against that fixture in `--release` mode first: no crash (0.25s, confirming a release build's smaller per-frame stack usage and/or larger effective stack keeps ~3,000 levels safe) -- an honest negative, not skipped.

Ran the identical, unfixed code in DEFAULT debug-profile mode (no `--release`, matching how every prior generation's own `cargo run -p atlas-cli`/`cargo test` validation commands in this session have actually been invoked): reliable crash, `thread '...' has overflowed its stack`, `fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting`, process exit via `signal: 6, SIGABRT` -- the exact documented failure signature this codebase already names for the analogous, already-fixed `syn` recursion bug.

Isolated every crash-inducing run inside its own `cargo test -- --ignored --exact <name>` subprocess invocation specifically so an actual SIGABRT would only terminate that isolated process, never this session's own shell or state -- confirmed safe by observing the Bash tool's own exit code/output return normally after each crash.

design_decisions.question: Depth-counting guard (mirroring `adapter::semantic::rust`'s text-heuristic `max_structural_recursion_risk`) or a dedicated large-stack thread (mirroring `EXTRACTION_STACK_SIZE`)?
design_decisions.decision: Depth-counting guard. Filesystem directory depth is EXACTLY countable (unlike source-text bracket nesting, which needs a heuristic scan to account for comments/string literals before a real parse), so an exact `depth: usize` parameter threaded through the existing mutual recursion is simpler, cheaper, and more precise than either a heuristic pre-scan or a large dedicated stack -- no new thread-spawning machinery needed, and the guard triggers deterministically at a known, chosen depth rather than probabilistically near whatever stack size happens to be available.

design_decisions.question: What depth limit, and how was it chosen (not merely picked arbitrarily)?
design_decisions.decision: 512, chosen with a wide empirical safety margin: the real crash was confirmed at ~600 levels in debug mode (this generation's own regression-test depth) and the walker's own maximum REACHABLE depth via its path-accumulating access pattern is naturally capped around ~2,000-3,000 by `PATH_MAX` regardless. 512 sits comfortably below every depth a real repository could ever legitimately need (this repository's own real directory nesting is nowhere close) while leaving a wide margin under the confirmed crash depth, matching the same 'safety margin over the actual empirically-confirmed risk' discipline already documented for `MAX_STRUCTURAL_RECURSION_RISK`.

design_decisions.question: Fix `visit_docs`/`visit_adl_sources` (adapter/src/lib.rs) too, given they share the identical unbounded-recursion shape (confirmed by direct reading, not merely trusting the prior audit's report)?
design_decisions.decision: No, deliberately deferred to a named follow-up, not bundled into this generation. Confirmed by direct reading that both functions share the exact same mutual-recursion-with-no-depth-bound shape as the now-fixed `visit_inventory`, making them very likely equally vulnerable -- but this generation's own falsification effort (the empirical crash reproduction, the fixture-construction technique, the depth-choice reasoning) was spent specifically on `visit_inventory`, and extending the same fix to two more call sites without independently falsifying each is exactly the kind of scope-widening the standing loop's own discipline warns against absorbing into one generation. Named explicitly as the next, already-scoped, cheap follow-up.

stable_validator_law_compliance.claim: A real repository's directory tree containing more than 512 levels of nested subdirectories can no longer crash the whole Atlas process via `adapter::source::visit_inventory` -- the walker stops recursing at that depth, records the directory as a resource-limited artifact (visible in the report, never silently dropped), and every other artifact in the repository is still accounted for normally.

implementation.code_change: adapter/src/source/mod.rs -- new `MAX_DIRECTORY_NESTING_DEPTH: usize = 512` constant with a doc comment naming the exact empirical falsification behind the chosen value. `classify_entry` and `visit_inventory` both gained a `depth: usize` parameter, threaded through their mutual recursion (`visit_inventory(root, &path, out, depth + 1)`); `classify_entry`'s directory arm now checks `depth >= MAX_DIRECTORY_NESTING_DEPTH` BEFORE recursing and, when exceeded, records the directory via the existing `classify_non_file` helper (`ArtifactKind::Special`, reason `"resource-limit: directory nesting depth exceeded"`) instead of recursing further -- mirroring the existing `record_unreadable_artifact`/`policy_boundary` recovery pattern already used for every other per-directory failure mode in this same function, never a silent drop.
